title: Process Chain Sensitivities in Green Steel Production: Tramp Element Impacts on Casting and Reheating
abstract: Abstract Surface defects are a critical indicator of semi-finished product quality, with the elements Cu and Sn exerting a significant influence through the phenomenon known as hot shortness. The present study quantifies the defect sensitivity caused by Cu and Sn for three different steel grades under continuous casting conditions using the In-situ Material Characterization by Bending (IMC-B) test. Building on this, purposefully pre-damaged samples were subjected to reheating under process-related conditions within a natural-gas combustion atmosphere. The objective is to investigate how surface defects from the casting process evolve depending on their initial depth and the selected final reheating temperature. Finally, metallographic analyses allow for a correlation between the initial defect depth and the surface morphology after reheating.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The transformation of steel production towards a more circular economy inevitably leads to an increased use of steel scrap. In certain cases, this may result in an increased content of undesirable tramp elements (particularly Cu and Sn), while remaining within the limits required to guarantee the mechanical and technological properties of the final product. Due to technical and economic limitations, these elements can hardly be removed in the metallurgical process, which may have a massive impact on subsequent process steps such as continuous casting, reheating, and hot rolling. The negative effects of Cu and Sn with regard to the formation of low-melting phases and the resulting surface defects are well documented and described [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. To summarize it briefly, while Fe oxidizes and forms scale, elements with a lower affinity to oxygen like Cu and Sn accumulate at the interface between steel and scale and at the surface near austenite grain boundaries. If the accumulation exceeds the solubility limit, (partly) liquid Cu-rich phases form. These significantly promote the formation of surface defects in subsequent processes, a phenomenon known as hot shortness. However, defects are not uniform in their impact as their effect on product quality depends largely on their point of origin. While casting defects may be eliminated during the reheating phase, those introduced during the rolling process inevitably result in quality issues on the semi-finished product.

This contribution aims to clarify how surface defects that have already developed during continuous casting affect subsequent reheating and descaling. The goal is to evaluate the surface condition before hot rolling and to define critical defect sizes from casting, which may lead to quality problems in the subsequent rolling steps. A particular focus is placed on the influence of the Si content. The experimental investigation in this study is carried out in two stages. First, crack formation is investigated using the In-situ Material Characterization by Bending (IMC-B) test. To ensure a distinctive defect formation, the investigated steels contain Cu and Sn [ 5 ]. Second, samples with defects from the IMC‑B test are subjected to oxidation experiments under process-near reheating cycles to analyze in detail the interaction between cracks and scaling.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: The focus in this investigation is set on three different steel grades with moderate additions of Cu and Sn. The chemical composition is summarized in Table  1 . P, S, and N are below 100, 40, and 60 ppm, respectively. The TRIP steel is micro alloyed with 0.02 wt.% Ti and Nb. MC represents a medium carbon construction steel, whereas MC (Si-free) corresponds to the same steel grade but without Si. In the first part of this investigation, samples with surface defects were produced using the IMC‑B test. The advantage of the IMC‑B test is that, due to the oxidizing conditions prevailing in the experiment, it exhibits high sensitivity to the tramp elements Cu and Sn [ 5 ]. Therefore, it can reliably produce defects, which is the prerequisite for the second part of this study. A detailed description of the IMC‑B test can be found in previous publications [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. The cooling cycle applied in this study is shown in Fig.  1  and focuses on bending at 1000 °C to ensure a distinct defect formation [ 5 ]. The experimental parameters are summarized in Table  2 . After the experiment the samples were slowly cooled to room temperature, descaled with diluted citric acid, and investigated for surface cracks in the strain-influenced area (crack distribution, morphology and depth) via a digital microscope (Keyence VHX7000). Also, the critical strain for first crack formation is defined. Those samples serve as a reference for the second part of the investigation in this study. In the second part of this investigation, samples with defects from the IMC‑B test were cooled to room temperature and then directly reheated (6 °C min −1 ) under a combustion atmosphere (λ ~ 1.11; 2 vol.% O 2 , 9 vol.% CO 2 , 18 vol.% H 2 O, 71 vol.% N 2 ) to either 1100 or 1200 °C and kept there for 120 min. In order to be as close to the real casting and reheating process as possible, descaling is omitted between the IMC‑B experiment and the reheating. After reheating, the samples were cooled to room temperature under ambient air. The applied reheating cycle is shown in Fig.  2 . The samples were then descaled with diluted citric acid and investigated for any remaining surface defects and compared to the reference samples from part 1. Fig. 2 Investigated reheating cycles

sections.heading: In-situ Material Characterization by Bending (IMC-B)
paragraphs: The results of the IMC‑B test in terms of the formed surface cracks are shown in Fig.  3  as a representative and interpretable crack intensity map where the area on the left and right of the bending axis is divided into eight equally sized sections, each containing four segments. In this evaluation, a white segment indicates a segment free of cracks, whereas yellow describes a segment with one to five cracks and red with more than five cracks. A hatched segment represents a very high crack number within this segment and the formation of network cracks and crack clusters. All three steels exhibit pronounced crack formation and a preferred formation of network cracks. Nevertheless, it is obvious that the TRIP steel shows a more favorable behavior than MC or MC (Si-free). The critical strain for first crack formation is around 1.5% for the TRIP steel, and below 1% for MC and MC (Si-free). Based on the literature [ 7 ,  8 ], the upper limit of mechanically induced strains for straightening is in the range of 1 to 2%. Therefore, all three steels should be considered critical for surface defect formation under the given parameters. Fig. 3 Crack intensity map and critical strain for the three investigated steels

Figure  4  illustrates the appearance of the sample surface with respect to the distance to the bending axis. As the applied strain on the sample surface decreases with increasing distance to the bending axis, cracks formation changes significantly over the sample surface. In a distance of 35 to 40 mm (section 1) to the bending axis, no cracks were formed for the TRIP steel, for MC first singular cracks can be noticed, whereas for MC (Si-free), beside singular cracks, also first network cracks appear. Lowering the distance to the bending axis to 25 to 30 mm (section 3) intensifies cracks formation for all three steels. Now the first singular defects were also evident for the TRIP steel. For MC and MC (Si-free) preferred network cracks were formed. Further reducing the distance to bending axis down to 10 to 15 mm (section 6) respectively 0 to 5 mm (section 8) strengthens crack formation significantly for all three investigated steels. However, it is obvious that TRIP shows the best and MC (Si-free) the worst behavior. Fig. 4 Appearance of the sample surface for the three investigates steels with respect to the distance to the bending axis:  a  to  d  TRIP;  e  to  h  MC;  i  to  l  MC (Si-free)

Figure  5  illustrates the average and max. crack depth for the three investigated steels. In each section the deepest ten cracks were measured. It is obvious that a higher strain (lower distance to the bending axis) increases the depth of formed cracks. For MC (Si free) cracks with a depth of up to 1500 µm were documented in the area of the bending axis, whereas it drops to roughly 800 µm for MC and 600 µm for TRIP. For MC and MC (Si-free) the differences can be clearly attributed to the presence of Si. Based on oxidation experiments, Si is known to counteract the negative effects of Cu-rich phases as it favors the entrapment of Cu-rich particles directly into the scale. However, this effect is mostly associated with temperatures in the range of 1150 °C and above [ 9 ,  10 ]. As the stripping temperature of the sample after the mold is roughly 1180 °C, the time frame, where the sample has a temperature high enough for this mechanism to take effect, is only a few seconds. Thus, the influence is noticeable but limited. For the TRIP steel the interpretation cannot be solely attributed to the higher presence of Si as it also differs for other alloying elements such as for example Al. As the TRIP steel is micro-alloyed, smaller grains are present on the sample surface, which may reduce the amount of Cu-rich phases at the grain boundaries and therefore leading to a reduction of the depth of formed surface cracks [ 11 ]. Fig. 5 Depth of formed surface defects with respect to the distance to the bending axis

sections.heading: Reheating of IMC-B Samples
paragraphs: Figure  6  shows the scale layer thickness after the reheating of 1100 and 1200 °C. The layer thickness is in the range of 1.5 mm for 1100 °C and up to 2 respectively 3 mm for 1200 °C. Independent of the final reheating temperature, MC (Si-free) shows the thickest scale. Scale detachments are visible, particularly for MC and TRIP, while the layer for MC (Si-free) is continuous. Fig. 6 Scale layer thickness after reheating for TRIP ( a  and  d ), MC ( b  and  e ) and MC (Si-Free) ( c  and  f ):  a  to  c  1100 °C;  d  to  f  1200 °C

Compared to the surface of the reference experiments (see Fig.  5 ), clear differences can be detected after the reheating tests. No surface defects can be seen on the TRIP steel for either reheating to 1100 or 1200 °C (see Fig.  7 a to d and Fig.  8 a to d). The surface is smooth with no noticeable roughness. For MC no traces of former defects can be identified for reheating to 1200 °C (see Fig.  8 e to h). The same applies for reheating to 1100 °C, except for the area of the bending axis, (see Fig.  7 e to h). Around the bending axis, a surface roughness with depths of up to 0.7 mm is noticeable, representing the remains of larger cracks. Apparently, the increased scaling of approximately half a millimeter at 1200 °C was enough to remove the last traces of former cracks. Oxidized grain boundaries with a depth of around 30 µm can be found across the entire surface for TRIP and MC, with a more intense formation for reheating to 1200 °C. Fig. 7 Appearance of the sample surface after reheating at 1100 °C for the three investigated steels with respect to the distance to the bending axis:  a  to  d  TRIP;  e  to  h  MC;  i  to  l  MC (Si-free) Fig. 8 Appearance of the sample surface after reheating at 1200 °C for the three investigated steels with respect to the distance to the bending axis:  a  to  d  TRIP;  e  to  h  MC;  i  to  l  MC (Si-free)

A different situation arises for MC (Si-free) (see Fig.  7 i to l and Fig.  8 i to l). The surface is without defects in sections 1 to 4, however a significant surface roughness due to the remains of bending cracks can be observed for sections 5 to 8. The roughness is partly more than 1 mm, which is practically identical to the maximum measured crack depth in the reference experiments (see Fig.  5 ). Furthermore, scale residues can still be detected at the base of these former cracks. Therefore, it can be concluded that descaling a rough surface is more difficult than descaling smooth surfaces, since the descaling time was the same for all samples and sections.

For TRIP and MC, isolated Cu phases can be discovered on the surface, while the entire surface of MC (Si-free) is covered with them. Compared to reheating at 1100 °C, Cu-rich phases are noticeable at the sample surface, but their intensity is reduced, which can be attributed to the higher temperature and the preferred entrapment of Cu-rich phases directly into the scale [ 12 ]. For both reheating temperatures, the higher tendency for the formation of Cu-rich phases at the steel surface in the absence of Si aligns well with literature [ 10 ].

Based on the results of the crack depth measurement taken after the bending test (see Fig.  5 ) and the location of surface roughness after reheating, a critical defect depth prior reheating of approximately 0.8 to 1 mm for reheating to 1100 °C and around 1 to 1.5 mm for reheating to 1200 °C can be estimated. Defects exceeding this size pose an increased risk of remaining on the surface and affecting subsequent processes, whereas smaller defects can be considered virtually uncritical as they will be completely removed by scaling.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook
paragraphs: All three examined steels show a high tendency to form surface defects, even at moderate concentrations of Cu and Sn. A direct comparison of two medium carbon construction steels, one with and the second without Si, clearly shows that the absence of Si leads to a significant intensification of crack formation. Based on the investigated reheating parameters and obtained results, a defect depth prior reheating of around 1 mm should be considered as a critical threshold for any potential remaining surface defects/roughness after reheating, which may pose a risk for rolling related defects. In addition, the remaining surface roughness makes descaling more difficult as scale residues are more likely to be observed in those remaining defects. The results further outlined that the absence of Si drastically enhances the formation of Cu-rich phases at the steel surface, which, if they are not removed during descaling, may result in difficulties in subsequent processes. These results offer a foundational understanding of how surface defect size influences reheating and descaling, establishing a robust framework for future research in the field.
